title: The Volkswagen, technology and folk culture as museum
summary: He recalls 1960 insularity and the computer; folk culture as museum.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: I had a Volkswagen in early 1960,

and my son was going to school in upstate New York. I went to visit him and went to a restaurant and came out and the thing was full of sputum. It was supposed to be patriotism at that time, it was very strong; it was unbelievable how really insular we were in early 1960. That's only twenty years ago.

I think the jet plane, the computer, the chip, changed everything. It brought everything--that was the thing that tipped it over. It was already there but without the computer, there could be no jet airplanes. None of that stuff would be; television couldn't have satellites up there.

For all that technology and its purpose, why are we using it, and I think that question really has to be answered. Unfortunately we don't have any thinkers in the avant garde there, who have been prepared for this; Marx certainly wasn't. Marx, as I understand it, has some nineteenth century concepts; if there are parts of it that

work today, great; but essentially it's a nineteenth century concept. It is always laisse faire. Neither of them really worked and I'm suppose to answer an article on folk music here and the guy says, put it into Soviet constitution that they should preserve these folk ways, it's very important, but that's one of the reasons Russia has built a wall around itself, that's true. But I bet you that it won't--it will become a museum quickly with this sort of--very much like the Indian cultures; they preserved the totem pole, they preserved the whole culture, encouraging this sort of thing, yet the culture has died, and it's that culture, the living culture, that's important. It's important to have it around, but it really is a museum.
It's like Pete Seeger's folk music.
